definition: Motion is the change in position of an object over time. An object is in motion if its position changes relative to a reference point.
examples: A car moving along a road is in motion relative to the ground.
A book on a table is at rest relative to the table.
common_misconceptions: Students may think an object is always in motion or always at rest, not realising motion depends on the reference point.

definition: Speed is the rate at which an object covers distance. It tells you how fast something is moving but not in which direction.
examples: If a car travels 100 km in 2 hours, its speed is 50 km/h.
A snail moving 0.01 m per second has a speed of 0.01 m/s.
common_misconceptions: Speed and velocity are the same — speed has no direction, velocity does.

definition: Velocity is speed in a specific direction. It is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude (speed) and direction.
examples: A car moving 60 km/h north has a velocity of 60 km/h north.
Two cars going opposite directions at 50 km/h have different velocities.
common_misconceptions: Velocity is just speed — students forget the direction component.
An object moving in a circle at constant speed has changing velocity because the direction changes.

definition: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time. An object accelerates when it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction.
examples: A car going from 0 to 100 km/h in 10 seconds has an acceleration of 10 km/h per second.
A ball thrown upward decelerates (negative acceleration) due to gravity.
common_misconceptions: Acceleration only means speeding up — it also includes slowing down (deceleration) and changing direction.
Zero acceleration means zero velocity — no, it means constant velocity.

definition: A force is a push or pull acting on an object. Forces can cause an object to start moving, stop moving, change speed, or change direction. Force is measured in Newtons (N).
examples: Pushing a shopping cart applies a force.
Gravity pulls objects toward the Earth.
common_misconceptions: A force is needed to keep an object moving — in reality, objects in motion stay in motion unless a force (like friction) acts on them.

definition: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted upon by a net external force. This is also called the law of inertia.
examples: A ball rolling on a flat surface eventually stops because of friction (an external force).
Passengers lurch forward when a bus suddenly stops because their bodies tend to keep moving.
common_misconceptions: Objects naturally come to rest — they actually continue moving unless a force like friction stops them.
Inertia is a force — inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

definition: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass. More force means more acceleration; more mass means less acceleration.
examples: Pushing a 2 kg box with 10 N of force gives an acceleration of 5 m/s².
A heavier truck needs more force than a car to achieve the same acceleration.
common_misconceptions: F = ma means force equals mass plus acceleration — it is mass times acceleration.
Heavier objects fall faster — in a vacuum all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass.

definition: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal force in the opposite direction on the first object.
examples: When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force.
A rocket moves forward by expelling gas backward.
common_misconceptions: Action and reaction forces cancel out — they act on different objects so they don't cancel.
The reaction force is weaker — it is always exactly equal in magnitude.

definition: Gravity is the force of attraction between any two objects that have mass. On Earth, gravity pulls objects toward the centre of the planet with an acceleration of approximately 9.8 m/s².
examples: A 50 kg student weighs about 490 N on Earth (50 × 9.8).
The same student would weigh less on the Moon because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
common_misconceptions: Mass and weight are the same — mass is the amount of matter, weight is the gravitational force on that mass.
There is no gravity in space — gravity exists everywhere, it just gets weaker with distance.

definition: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity. It describes how hard it is to stop a moving object. Momentum is a vector — it has both size and direction.
examples: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s has a momentum of 20,000 kg·m/s.
A fast bullet has high momentum despite small mass because of high velocity.
common_misconceptions: Momentum and force are the same — momentum is a property of a moving object, force is what changes momentum.

definition: Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force. Work is measured in Joules (J). No work is done if the object does not move.
examples: Pushing a box 5 m with 20 N of force does 100 J of work.
Carrying a bag while walking horizontally does no work against gravity.
common_misconceptions: Holding a heavy object is doing work — no work is done unless the object moves in the direction of the force.

definition: Energy is the ability to do work. It comes in many forms: kinetic (motion), potential (stored), thermal (heat), light, sound, electrical, and chemical. Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transformed from one form to another.
examples: A moving ball has kinetic energy.
A stretched rubber band has elastic potential energy.
Food contains chemical energy that your body converts to kinetic energy.
common_misconceptions: Energy can be used up — energy is transformed, not destroyed.
Only moving objects have energy — stationary objects can have potential energy.

definition: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. It is measured in Watts (W). One Watt equals one Joule per second.
examples: A 60 W light bulb uses 60 Joules of energy every second.
Lifting a box quickly requires more power than lifting it slowly, even though the work done is the same.
common_misconceptions: Power and energy are the same — power is the rate of energy use, energy is the total amount.

definition: Sound is a longitudinal wave that travels through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) by compressing and expanding the particles. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
examples: Sound travels faster in water (~1500 m/s) than in air (~340 m/s).
You cannot hear sound in outer space because there is no medium.
common_misconceptions: Sound travels through a vacuum — it needs a medium (particles) to propagate.
Sound travels faster than light — light is much faster (~300,000 km/s vs ~340 m/s in air).

definition: Frequency is the number of wave cycles per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive identical points on a wave. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength and vice versa.
examples: A radio station at 100 MHz has a frequency of 100,000,000 cycles per second.
Red light has a longer wavelength (~700 nm) than blue light (~450 nm).
common_misconceptions: Frequency and wavelength are the same thing — they are inversely related.
Amplitude affects frequency — amplitude affects loudness/intensity, not frequency.
